name: libfreenect
desc: Drivers and libraries for the Xbox Kinect device
why: Drivers for the Xbox Kinect, letting you read depth and IR streams from a cheap sensor over USB.

brief.what_it_is: libfreenect is a userspace driver library for the Microsoft Kinect (the original Xbox 360 model, per the firmware note about model 1414). It takes data from the sensor over USB and exposes RGB and depth images, motor tilt, accelerometer, LED, and audio. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows, and ships C, C++, C#, Python, Ruby, ActionScript, and Java (JNA) wrappers plus a set of demo viewers such as freenect-glview and freenect-wavrecord. The README does not mention infrared streams, although the scout note says it does.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no explicit motivation. It describes the project as a userspace driver for the Microsoft Kinect, maintained by the OpenKinect community, and points users of the newer Kinect v2 (Xbox One) to the separate libfreenect2 project.
brief.how_it_works: The library talks to the device over libusb (1.0.18 or later; 1.0.22 or later on Windows) and is built with CMake. The fakenect component can record a live session to a directory and later replay it by preloading libfakenect.so with LD_PRELOAD and pointing FAKENECT_PATH at the recording, so programs can run without the hardware attached.

brief.install_notes: Linux needs the udev rules from platform/linux/udev installed. Ubuntu's packaged version may be very old, so the README points to the wiki for newer builds. On Windows, use Zadig to install the libusbK driver for each device, and pass CMake the libusb include and library paths. Examples need OpenGL and glut (included on macOS), freeglut3-dev, libxmu-dev and libxi-dev on Debian-family systems, and pthreads-win32 on Windows. Audio and, on newer models, motor and LED control need firmware uploaded to the device; the README suggests inserting it at runtime just after freenect_init(). Gentoo ebuilds and Arch AUR PKGBUILDs are also mentioned.
brief.standout: Fakenect lets you record a real Kinect session and replay it through an unmodified program by swapping the USB driver with LD_PRELOAD, which is a neat way to test vision code without the hardware. The project also covers the whole device (motors, LED, accelerometer, audio), not just the video streams.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched README has no release date, version number or last-commit date, and I did not fetch the releases page or commit history. The content looks current (it names libusb 1.0.22 and CMake 3.12.4 minimums and points to the libfreenect2 successor), but I cannot confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: The homepage https://openkinect.org/ returned HTTP 525, so the brief relies on the GitHub README. Firmware may not be legal to redistribute in some jurisdictions, as the README warns. Audio and some motor/LED features depend on uploaded firmware. Windows needs Zadig and a specific libusb version. The wrappers are described as not guaranteed to be API stable or up to date. The README does not claim infrared support, which the scout note mentions. Kinect v2 hardware is out of scope and needs libfreenect2.

entry.title: libfreenect
entry.tldr: A userspace driver that turns an original Xbox 360 Kinect into a USB depth camera, with demo viewers and a record-and-replay trick for working without the hardware.
entry.deeper_look:
libfreenect is the OpenKinect community's userspace driver for the Microsoft Kinect. It talks to the sensor over libusb and exposes RGB and depth images, motor tilt, accelerometer, LED, and audio. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows, with wrappers for C, C++, C#, Python, Ruby, ActionScript, and Java. The README says the wrappers are not guaranteed to be API stable or up to date.

The Homebrew formula installs a set of small demo programs alongside the library. `freenect-glview` shows the camera streams, `freenect-tiltdemo` moves the motor, `freenect-micview` and `freenect-wavrecord` handle the microphone array, and `freenect-regview` looks at depth-to-colour registration. They work as a quick tour of what the device exposes, and as example code.

The interesting part is fakenect. `fakenect-record` saves a live Kinect session into a directory. Later you launch an unmodified program with `LD_PRELOAD` pointing at `libfakenect.so` and `FAKENECT_PATH` pointing at the recording. The program believes a Kinect is attached and gets the recorded frames. That is a neat way to develop and test vision code without the sensor, and it shows how library interposition can stand in for hardware.

This covers only the original Xbox 360 Kinect. The README sends owners of the newer Kinect v2 (Xbox One) to the separate libfreenect2 project.
entry.install:
brew install libfreenect
# Needs an original Xbox 360 Kinect plugged in over USB (the README also mentions `brew install --HEAD libfreenect` for the latest code).
# On Linux, the README says to install the udev rules from platform/linux/udev.

try_this.what_happens: Opens the demo viewer showing the live RGB and depth streams from a connected Kinect.
Records a live Kinect session into the session directory for later playback.
Replays the recorded session through the viewer with no Kinect attached.

entry.whats_unique: Fakenect records a real sensor session and replays it into unmodified programs by swapping the driver with LD_PRELOAD. The library also covers the whole device (motor, LED, accelerometer, audio), not only the video.
entry.caveats: Needs a first-generation Kinect to do anything live. Audio and some motor and LED features need firmware uploaded to the device, which the README warns may not be legal to redistribute in some jurisdictions. The homepage returned an error when checked, and recent project activity could not be confirmed.
